observation_summary: The LookupTranslator fails to correctly translate CharSequence inputs that are not Strings (e.g., StringBuffer or CharBuffer) because it relies on HashMap lookups using CharSequence keys, which do not guarantee consistent equals/hashCode behavior across different implementations.
reasoning_summary: The root cause is the reliance on a HashMap with CharSequence keys, which is fundamentally flawed because CharSequence implementations (like String vs. StringBuffer) do not guarantee equality or consistent hash codes. The fix requires changing the lookup strategy (the algorithm) to handle these types correctly, rather than just adding a guard or changing a single value. It is not a design-level capability omission (Function/Class/Object) because the translator is intended to work with CharSequence, but the internal implementation of the lookup algorithm is insufficient for the contract of the CharSequence interface.
evidence_used: The core of org.apache.commons.lang3.text.translate is a HashMap<CharSequence, CharSequence> lookupMap.
CharSequence interface does not refine the general contracts of the equals and hashCode methods.
CharBuffer.equals is documented that a char buffer is not equal to any other type of object.
The failing test shows that the translator fails to consume the input when a StringBuffer is provided.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The capability to translate CharSequence is present, but the internal implementation (the lookup algorithm) is flawed for the provided input types.
The issue is not a mismatch in the interface signature, but rather the internal implementation's reliance on an unsafe assumption about the CharSequence contract.
